utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please be seated? Could we ask the usher to have the accused brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear me? Are there any technical problems? Does the Defence hear? Does Mr. Blaskic-once he puts his headset on, Mr. Blaskic, do you hear me? Do you hear me, Mr. Blaskic. GENERAL BLASKIC: Good morning, your Honour. I hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor? Have they fixed all the technical problems? All right. That's good. We can resume at the point where Mr. Cayley stopped yesterday. We resume therefore at 10 o'clock, and we should have a pause around 11 o'clock or 11.15. 11.15, that would allow everybody to rest up a bit but without having to interrupt any testimony. I give you the floor, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. The Prosecutor would like to continue, with your permission, Mr. President, with Dr. Zoran Pajic. (Witness enters court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, profess off. Would you settle yourself in, as you did yesterday? Please be seated. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. While the witness is getting his paperwork ready, if I could just remind everybody in the court where we are at the moment in the course of Dr. Pajic's testimony. We are presently referring to exhibits 38A, B and C, which are the extracts chosen by Dr. Pajic from the Narodna list. You will remember there are three different versions of this. Yesterday we terminated at page 37 in the English and Croatian version and page 40 in the French version. That is grey tab number 2 on the side of the file, so grey tab number 2, page 37 and page 40 respectively. Dr. Pajic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. (In interpretation): yes, I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to page 40 -- rather page 37 in your edition -- which is specifically titled "Rules of military discipline", without going into particular detail in this extensive document, I would like you to generally explain its structure and purpose to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is a collection of rules and military discipline and, as I said yesterday, your Honour, I can speak about this document only as a lawyer, that is to say without going into the military terminology involved, and the professional military contents of this document. So from that point of view I can say, first of all, that this is an unusually extensive document, which shows the legislator, or rather the people who worked on this piece of legislation devoted special attention to the rules of military discipline, which is the original title, because I believe that if this is not the longest document that I had the opportunity of analysing, it is definitely one of the longest and most extensive ones. It even has 112 Articles. In this document we find, first of all, provisions on very clear rules regarding the breaking of discipline. There is a special section on sanctions. The procedure has been elaborated in detail, and there are many material provisions. So from the point of view of legal procedure and material procedure this is a very detailed document, and, finally, there is the structure of military disciplinary courts too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, what is the date of this document? When did it come into force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is dated 3rd July 1992. It was signed by the President of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, so it is one single person who signed this document in both capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Does this document, as you have stated before, show a consistent structure based on subordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to repeat once again, although I said this several times during my testimony yesterday, that this is again a very consistent document, which fully shows how much the principle of subordination has been carried out completely, a clear hierarchy in terms of carrying military discipline in the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and may I reiterate again, as a lawyer, I invariably have the impression that this is an excellent example of legal skills in terms of elaborating these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. If you have nothing further to say about that document, if I can take you to page 53 in the Croatian and English text, and page 60 in the French, which is a decision on establishing the criteria for defining confidential defence data and special and general procedures for their protection. If you could make some general comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decision on establishing the criteria for defining confidential defence data and special and general procedures for their protection. Also this is a rather extensive document in view of the subject matter regulated by it. There are 24 Articles in it. I believe it is characteristic. It should be highlighted. The introduction, the introductory section of this document shows that the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna function in practice, the decree establishing them. Article 10, paragraph 4, HZ H-B, the function for adopting such a document was delegated to the head of the Defence department. The Head of the Defence Department was entrusted with adopting such a document and signing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. I hope that this is the right document I have in front of me. You are talking about 10, paragraph 4. I do not have an Article 10, paragraph 4. Perhaps I'm making an error here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is actually referring to a previous document, which was the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community, which commences at page 12 in the English text, and he is referring to Article 10 of that text, which empowered certain officials within the HVO to pass what I would call in English terminology delegated legislation. I will just ensure it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What decree are you talking about? Could you tell me because I do not really see it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, page 12 of the French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's Article 10 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Page 4, what's being discussed is the structure of the command -- the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Article 10, line 4, the structure of command and control of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if you would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for this bit of confusion that was created. Perhaps I didn't state clearly enough why I'm referring to the decree of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I refer to this decree because it is mentioned in the preamble to the decision on establishing the criteria for defining confidential defence data. The reason I mentioned this first was because I wished to point out that the system that is elaborated on the decree on the armed forces from July 1992 functions in practice, that is to say that certain departments of the Croatian Defence Council took over the functions given to them by this previous decree of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and they function according to the principle of delegated responsibility. I should repeat briefly that on the basis of these principles this decision was signed by the head of the department for defence of the HVO, not by the head of the HVO personally, as was previously the case. As concerns the contents of this decision, I should say that the system itself was elaborated, the rules and criteria and standards, as to what confidential data are, who has the right to handle confidential data and at what level certain confidential data can be made available to certain persons. I wish to draw your attention to Article 13 specifically, where there are different degrees of confidentiality. It says that: "Every information which is an official secret depending on its importance shall be classified according to one of the following degrees of confidentiality: strictly confidential, confidential or internal". If we look at the legal and administrative legacy of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say that certain officials at certain levels had access either to strictly confidential or confidential or only internal papers, depending on the post they held. That would be all I have to say on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if you could now move on to page 59 in your edition, that is page 67 in the French and page 59 in the Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, Judge Shahabuddeen would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, just before you move on, could I attract your attention to what I believe was the last provision you referred to? I think that was Article 13. More particularly I'm referring to the second line on the first paragraph in which there's a reference to the security and defence of the country. The country there would be what country and the official secrets there would be official secrets as between what country and any other country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may have a minute to read it, please ... (Pause.) If I understood your question correctly, your Honour, this is the protection of data that are important for defence, and if they were to be revealed, it could impair the security and defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So when it says "country", what is meant is the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So the secrets which are enjoined by that provision would include secrecy as between even the Croatian Community and the Government of the overall Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would it? I'm not sure I understand. In other words, if an official of the Croatian Community were to divulge information to the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would that be caught by the prohibition in that provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way I understand Article 13, this would be a grave breach of secrecy of protected data, data protected by this provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, just to clarify the point that Dr. Shahabuddeen is making, if I could refer you to Article 2 of this decision, which I think makes it quite clear who the proprietor of this confidential information is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. It is Article 2 where it says and I quote: "Confidential defence data shall be deemed to be data important to defence originating from the sphere of competence from the administrative bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and legal bodies, the discovery of which may cause harm to the security of HZ H-B".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm content.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I can refer you to page 59 of the Croatian edition, that is page 67 of the French, if you could very briefly make some comments on this document. I think it also demonstrates the principle of delegated legislation under Article 10, paragraph 4 of the decree on armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Defence Department or the head of the Defence Department issues the rules and the military identification card, identifying the members of the military of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that's to say those who serve in the armed forces. Article 1 says: "Members of the HZ H-B shall be issued a military identification card". The military ID is a public document attesting to membership in the HZ H-B army. So this is the way in which the members of the armed forces of the HZ H-B are identified within the armed forces and vis-à-vis the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom is the document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic in his capacity as Head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to page 60 of your text, page 60 in the English and Croatian versions and page 68 in the French, this is a mandatory directive on the enforcement of penal sanctions for acts committed against the armed forces of the HZ H-B. Could you briefly explain this document and give the court your comments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, this is a document which on the basis of the previous authority I referred to was issued by the Head of the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is a mandatory directive, and its exact title is "Mandatory Directive on the Application of Current Regulations and Possible Pronouncement of Penal Sanctions for Acts Committed against the Armed Forces of HZ H-B". I shall refer to this document very briefly. It is important, because it shows in practice also not only on the basis of the documents that I reviewed and that I quoted here until now, but it is obvious that in practice, too, military discipline was supervised and controlled and in the process of this supervision 37 types of breach or violation were listed, the first four paragraphs of the text. On this basis one can see that indeed the Defence Department was in charge of the military discipline in the armed forces of the HZ H-B and adopted certain directives in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The date of this document is 14th August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a copy where the signature has been crossed out. Does this have any specific meaning, Professor? I think this is something my colleagues have picked up as well. You can see it has been crossed out. Does it have any special meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can explain this. There was a typographical error in the translation in that the name of "Bruno Stojic, Department of Defence" was incorporated into the English and French versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not get the translation here. I mean, I'm not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it is in effect a correction to make it absolutely identical to the original version, to the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you, Dr. Pajic, to page 62 of the bundle before you, which is page 70 in the French, and I think you can actually deal with the next four documents, five documents together, these are decisions on appointing various officials within the departments of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have before me a few decisions on personnel matters, appointments of individuals to certain posts within the HVO, and, finally, a decision on the appointment of the members of the commission for certificates for elementary and secondary schools on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What these documents have in common are that they were all signed by the President of the HVO, who was at the same time the President of the HZ H-B, namely Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think they all demonstrate the principle of delegated authority from the preambular paragraph in that the official appointing was actually utilising legislation that had been previously passed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if you have no further comments on the first volume, we can now move on to document 3, and that, your Honours -- the number of the document is indicated by the grey tabs on the spine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like clarification from the Professor. On page 75, the last decision, could you make a very brief comment which would explain why the four individuals named as heads of the departments are responsible for drafting formulas and diplomas in primary and secondary schools? Would you have a comment to make in answer to that question? It seems at least theoretically to be kind of unusual. This is a very troubled period. Then one sees these four individuals who are going to be in charge of forms having to do with the diplomas. It is really a clarification I'm asking for. Just answer quickly please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand this decision within the context of the overall efforts to build up a State structure within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which would through its legislation and legal order cover all walks of life, including the drafting of certificate forms for school certificates. I think that is the only way to explain this. This was probably given such importance because in the drafting of these forms the wish was to reflect certain cultural and national characteristics which were given priority when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed, but I agree with you, Mr. President, that it is rather unusual at a time of war and wartime environment to come across this type of decision in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Cayley, go ahead, unless there are any other questions from the bench. No. All right. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could now refer you, Dr. Pajic, to document 3, which is the decree on District Military Prosecutors Offices, published in November 1992 and dated 17th October 1992, this document, I believe, established a military prosecution service within the territory of Herceg-Bosna. I wondered if you could make some comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my testimony yesterday I pointed out that the Croatian Defence Council held control over the legislative, executive and administrative powers, and yesterday I made a brief comment on the document dealing with misdemeanours and breaches in the armed forces, and I qualified that document as the first, though a modest step towards the take-over or rather the establishment of control over the judiciary by the Croatian Defence Council. This decree, which was passed on 17th October 1992 on District Military Prosecutors Offices of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is a step further on building up an autonomous legal system in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and we shall see later on that there is a continuity of effort in that direction so that the judicial system should be subjected to this centralised authority, the principle of unity of authority within the hands of the HVO in the Herceg-Bosna community. I should like to draw your attention to Article 7, which says that: "The District Military Prosecutor and his deputies shall be appointed by the HZ H-B Presidency at the proposal of the Head of the Defence Department". I should like to recall that the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is composed of representatives of the Croatian Defence Council, as I pointed out yesterday, when referring to the revised text on the formation of the Croatian Defence Council, dated July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to Article 4 of the decree, which I think states to whom the District Military Prosecutors were responsible for their work, could you make some comments about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 4, paragraph 3, clearly says that, and I quote: "The District Military Prosecutor shall be responsible for his work to the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the Presidency both appointed the District Military Prosecutor, the District Military Prosecutor was responsible to the Presidency, and, as you said, a constituent part of the Presidency was the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a correct conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 4, which is a decision on the establishment of border crossings with The Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very interesting decision and it covers the question of border crossings with The Republic of Croatia. In connection with this decision I should like to remind your Honours that the only two internationally recognised states in this area, that is the area of the border crossing mentioned in this decision, is The Republic of Croatia, on the one hand, and The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the other. I find it to be extremely unusual and strange that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna should pass a decision unilaterally or autonomously on border crossings with The Republic of Croatia. I stress again that this is a borderline between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia. This decision was passed on 12th November 1992, which means more than six months after the international recognition of both The Republic of Croatia and of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when both were admitted to the United Nations in May of that same year. After reading this, my conclusion is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna unilaterally virtually appropriated the border crossings between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia and by this independent decision designated those border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to the recitals of this decision pursuant to Article 18 of the statutory decision on the temporary organisation of executive authority, is this another example of delegated authority at work within this structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this occasion the signatory of the decision is the President of the Croatian Defence Council, Dr. Jadranko Perlic, who was in the meantime appointed President of the HVO, and this decision was passed on the basis of authority delegated to the HVO as a real government or ministerial cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now refer you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, your conclusion as to this document indicates that the Government of, or the so called Government of HZ H-B considered the borders as the borders of Bosnia itself, so it means that it extends, it considers itself as extensive in all the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would that be your conclusion, or is there any other text or provisions clarifying the borders of the Croatian -- the Bosnia Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My conclusion is that the Croatian Defence Council, acting as the supreme executive body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, took this decision on the establishment of border crossings along the frontier line between two sovereign states, The Republic of Croatia and The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This implies that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna simply appropriated a frontier belt and took over authority over that frontier belt from The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because logic would indicate that these frontier crossings can be designated only by decision of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina based in Sarajevo. If I may continue, there is no example in theory or practice of international law of any regional communities within a certain state determining border crossings with other sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you conclude that the Croatian Community considered its borders as the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself and that they should -- they had no strict borders of themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe in the opposite. By this decision the Croatian Community is rejecting the fact that this border is the border between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia, and it appropriates this border as its own, which implies that the Croatian Community sees itself as a sovereign state, which is now situated -- if I may refer to the map we saw yesterday, it is between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia, along this border area referred to in this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to be more clarified. If I understand you rightly, they do not consider that the party between -- the space between the Croatian Community and Croatia as separate from them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This decision wants to show, in fact, that the Croatian Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign entity with respect to The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and is declaring border crossings by itself towards The Republic of Croatia, completely ignoring the sovereignty of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that particular border area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I thought it was ignoring the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, not only the borders. It is speaking of the borders of Bosnia as its own borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is ignoring the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and implicitly it is ignoring that there exists a borderline between The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and The Republic of Croatia in that particular area, and it wants to proclaim that that area belongs to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If it would assist, Dr. Pajic, I have the map for you there, so you can demonstrate visually what we are talking about here to assist Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question. Well, first we could finish with the map in respect of the question that was asked by Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen would like to ask a question. Professor, would you first try to answer my colleague's question as completely as possible before moving to the question that Judge Shahabuddeen would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have the exhibit identified, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies to my learned friend. It's Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the first that we saw. We have to grant this objection. We have to identify the exhibit so that the Defence can be sure about what it wants to ask during its cross-examination. Professor, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I needed a little time to master this equipment, but may I show you briefly what we are talking about on this map? You see that the south-western border of what is outlined here as the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna borders, in fact, on The Republic of Croatia. On this map you do not see The Republic of Croatia, but this entire area south-west of this border on the map is, in fact, The Republic of Croatia. By this decision which we are analysing now the HVO of HZ H-B determines frontier crossings between the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and The Republic of Croatia. In the territory between the municipalities of Tomislavgrad and Imotski -- I should like to draw your attention on this map we have the old name of the municipality of Tomislavgrad as "Duvno". This name was changed, as far as I remember, in 1990 from "Duvno" to "Tomislavgrad". Beneath the letter "Z" you see the name "Duvno", which is now called Tomislavgrad within the Croatian Community, and on its western or south-western side it borders on the municipality of Imotski, which is a municipality within The Republic of Croatia. Going further south, we see that the next border crossing has been designated in the territory of the municipality of Posusje. There's a printing error here. It should be P-O-S-U-S, with an accent, J-E. It borders on the municipality of Imotski, therefore the same municipality within the territory of Croatia. Further south we come to the municipality of Grude, one of the component municipalities of the Croatian Community, which also borders on The Republic of Croatia. On the other side of the border is the municipality of Imotski. The next border crossing is in the territory of the municipality of Ljubuski bordering on the municipality of Vergoraz in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Finally, clearly there are two border crossings between the municipality of Ljubuski on the one hand and the municipality of Vergoraz in the Republic of Croatia, and finally along the same borderline between The Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the territory of the municipality of Kaplina on the side of the Croatian Community and the municipality of Metkovic in the territory of the Republic of Croatian on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I have a brief question which runs like this. We have listened to your testimony which moves in the direction of establishing that a separate state with accompanying state apparatus was being built up in the HZ H-B under the aegis of the HVO. In proof of that interpretation you point to the fact that the south-western boundary of the HZ H-B was congruent with the south-western boundary of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the HZ H-B established certain border crossings along that frontier, which was the international frontier between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. You referred to that as an act of appropriation. Now, the question which I have is whether similar border crossings were or were not established by the HZ H-B along those parts of its frontier with the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand completely your question, and indeed from the documentation placed at my disposal in the period covered by the document that I analysed there is no analogous decision of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the establishment of border crossings or a borderline of The Republic of Herceg-Bosna. If you are asking me for an explanation, I can just guess. In this period, that is the period of 1992-1993, the situation was still not quite clear, and there were some hesitant -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna hesitated to break off relations with The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As in this case, in addition the signatory, the President of the HVO HZ H-B, you find names referring to The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the one hand, The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is still the only internationally recognised state in this part that we are talking about. On the other hand, there is an obvious need for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to create an impression in relation to third parties of apparent loyalty to The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which will gradually weaken and will become less in subsequent documents, particularly those dating from 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, would you go on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Pajic, if I could now refer you to document 5, which is a decision on the import of goods from The Republic of Croatia and I wondered if you could make some brief comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this decision, to put it quite briefly, preferential treatment is accorded to goods that are imported from The Republic of Croatia or goods originating from The Republic of Croatia. Special provisions are applied in terms of customs tariffs that are applied in the case of such goods. Again, the general conclusion that I can draw from this decision is that preferential treatment is accorded and it is a well-known fact that preferential treatment in international trade can only be accorded by a State to a State, not by entities that are not states to other states.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 6, which is the decision on the structure of the Home Guard, could you make some brief comments about this document, and in particular I would like you to refer to Articles 3 and 5 of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on the structure of the Home Guard was passed by the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and this decision actually stipulates that the Home Guard as a special form of territorial defence is established according to the territorial principle, and Article 3 that you mentioned shows that the Home Guard and I quote: " ... shall be comprised of all local reserve units of the armed forces of the HZ H-B and of new local units formed according to the territorial principle". As regards the chain of command, I draw your attention to Article 5, which clearly shows and I quote: " ... that units and headquarters of the Home Guard shall be subordinated to the commands of operational zones and to the general staff in the chain of command". That is to say that once these units start operating they fall under the chain of command of the operational zones and the general staff. The elaboration of these regulations is given according to Article 7 to the Defence Department of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 7, which is a decree on the coat of arms and flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war and the immediate threat of war. It's a fairly detailed document, but if you could draw the court's attention to the provisions which are specific to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion the point of the decree on the coat of arms and flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war is to state clearly the identity, the external identity and marks of this community. Therefore, we will see in Article 8 a very detailed elaboration on the rules governing the use of the coat of arms of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Not to quote all of this Article, but it is stated quite clearly on what occasions and on what documents the coat of arms of Herceg-Bosna would be used, and also in Article 11 the flag of the HZ H-B, when it will be displayed: "At all times on the premises of all HZ H-B bodies, on national holidays, on days of mourning", etc. It also says that: "Ships and other vessels shall fly the flag of the HZ H-B". So this is truly a document which is supposed to complete this picture of the HZ H-B as an independent entity. That is how I explain this. Heraldic experts could probably say a lot more about this. What is important is that there is a special chapter of this decree on punitive provisions, penalties, and in Croatian Dinars they stipulate the fines that are to be paid by a legal person if they violate the rules and the coat of arms and flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought, Professor, that you would try to explain the title of this decree. During your answer to Judge Shahabuddeen's questions you showed the process that was going on, but this decree seems to restrict the separatist notions. This has to do with imminent war danger or war itself. Could you give us an explanation of that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your question as one related to the time when this decision was passed. The 18th November 1992 was when it was passed. Of course, its intention is precisely in times of war, the immediate threat of war, to give immediate identification of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Finally, we see that many of these documents that I am quoting include this in their titles "in times of war or the immediate threat of war", because, as far as I know, that is the environment in which this entity was being created and where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Your evidence is directed to a process of building up a State, and you identified a while ago a discrepancy between the establishment of border crossings on one side as against a non-establishment of similar border crossings on the other side, and now we are dealing with flags. Now, we know, and I take it we accept, a recent example illustrates that, that a province could have a distinctive flag without that necessarily being intended to construe constitutional separatism. Now here we have your evidence, backed up by this document, that the Croatian Community instituted its own flag, and that flag was to be displayed on certain occasions. Was there any regulation within the Croatian Community about the permissibility of flying on official occasions the flag of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in a single document out of all that were made available to me was any mention made of an obligation or right to fly the flag of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They speak exclusively of the symbols, namely the coat of arms and the flag of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I avail myself of this opportunity to recall that in the tradition of the former Yugoslavia there were regional flags, flags of the republics that were members of the Yugoslav Federation. However, whenever these flags, regional flags, to call them regional flags on this occasion, were flown, there was always a legal obligation to fly at the same time the federal flag next to the flag of The Republic concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Pajic, if I could briefly refer you back to a document, document 6, on the decision of the structure of the Home Guard and its subordination, I wonder if you could just give the court the date of that document, when that document actually came into force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on the structure of the Home Guard enters into force on the day of issue, and that day is 3rd November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Pajic, if we could now move ahead to document 8, which is a decree on the manufacture of arms and military equipment within the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is a significant document and I wondered if you could make your general comments on this document to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to a technical detail here. First of all, you will see that this decree was published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna number 2 of January 1993. If you look at the date when this decision was passed, that is the 6th December 1993. I believe that this is a typographical error, namely this document was published in January 1993. So I imagine that it was adopted in December 1992. Just a small correction. To go back to the substance of the document now, the decree on the manufacture and trade of arms and military equipment in times of immediate threat of war or wartime in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is the document stipulating the manufacture, trade, provision and services in the domain of arms and military equipment, as well as business transactions. Management, financial and other aspects and other services related to the manufacture and trade of arms and military equipment are proclaimed as activities of special public interest of the HZ H-B. Article 2 stipulates that only those companies can be involved in this production which have the needed facilities for that kind of production, and which have obtained approval from the Croatian Defence Council. Further on, in Article 3, it is stipulated that companies that were previously registered for military production continue to operate as public companies for the manufacture of arms and military equipment. I wish to remind you of a document that I referred to yesterday on public corporations, public enterprises, where I said that this meant ethisation of former social ownership. So such enterprises were put under the control of the HVO in the HZ H-B, and this is now specifically stipulated for military facilities, and the most important public companies for the manufacture of military equipment and arms are listed here, and they are put under the control of the HVO. First of all, I wish to highlight that these are appropriate facilities in Vitez, Kiseljak, Travnik, Novi Travnik, then Mostar, Bugojno and Konjic, and that would complete the list. So these are military industrial complexes inherited from the former Yugoslavia, which remained naturally on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina when the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia fell apart, and now the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna proclaims these enterprises to be their own public enterprises. This is the well-known aircraft industry of Soko in Mostar; then in Novi Travnik a factory of machinery and hydraulics; Slobodan Prinsip Seljo in Vitez, I think this is a chemical industry; then the factory in Travnik; then Vitezite in Vitez; Slavko Radic in Bugojno; Igman in Konijc; then two enterprises in Varic; Optic Mechanics also belonging to the big company of Zrak. The headquarters of this company were in Sarajevo before and this facility was in Kiseljak. In Kiseljak there was also another part of the big Zrak company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to suspend our hearing until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume our hearing. Please be seated and have the accused brought in. Mr. Cayley, have your witness brought in and we can then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Pajic, if I could now refer you to document 9 in the bundle, which is the decree on the application of the law on regular courts in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Would you please give your comments on this document to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of this decree is the decree on the application of the law on regular courts in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war. Actually, this is a rather unusual title, because it introduces into practice a law on regular courts of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which will be applied in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna according to the law unless the provisions of that law contravene this decree. How can this be explained? In my opinion this is a simplified take-over of the law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and especially its procedural provisions, which are quite acceptable, and which can be applied and used in the practice of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What I consider to be particularly important in this decree is Article 2 and I quote: "In the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna courts shall be established and abolished by the decree of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna". Actually Article 2 puts an end to the authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina over the judicial system in Herceg-Bosna, because it is by decision of the Croatian Community that courts may be established and abolished. What is more, the number of judges, according to Article 4, is also determined by the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community, and, finally, Article 5 says that: "Judges and lay judges shall be elected and dismissed by the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna". My conclusions on the basis of this decree, as we are talking about regular courts, not military courts, my conclusion is that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna through the Presidency and the HVO is actually taking over control over the judicial function. I should like to recall that their control over the legislative, administrative and all defence affairs has already been established, and now, finally, it is the regular courts that are also placed under the full control of Herceg-Bosna, and it is particularly important to note that it is under the control of the Presidency and the Croatian Defence Council, which shows that the Croatian Defence Council actually has control overall state powers, legislative, judicial and every other. The document was passed on 23rd December 1992, and signed by the President of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Dr. Jadranko Perlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How do you interpret the fact that a decree can invalidate a law? At the same time it puts into force the law on ordinary courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The same decree seems to have a value which is greater than that of the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can understand your question. It has to do with the hierarchy of legal documents, where indeed a law would be superior to a decree, because a decree is in the hierarchy lower than a law, but I have no explanation for this. This is obviously a decree which introduces the law on regular courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you, Dr. Pajic, to document 10, which is a further decree on border crossing and traffic in the border areas of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, if you could give your comments on this document and include, as you've done before, the date of the document and the signatory to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is dated 26th February 1993. It is signed by the President of the Croatian Defence Council of HZ H-B, Dr. Perlic, again. It is a decree on border crossings and traffic in the border area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war. I should like to draw your attention to Article 7, which says that: "The HVO of the HZ H-B shall designate the international border crossings and the local border crossings". I have two observations to make in connection with this Article 7. The first is that prima facie this is a state act, because only a state can designate border crossings for international traffic and for local border traffic. In no state is that the responsibility of any regional community of municipalities. This is, therefore, a state-like act, which the Croatian Defence Council has assumed. My second observation is linked to your question, your Honour, as to whether there are border crossings along the northern border area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. They were not designated by this degree, but there is a reference to border crossings without any specification, border crossings of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and not solely border crossings with The Republic of Croatia. So this is a more general provision, which could serve as a legal basis for determining border crossings with The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the northern borders of the entity. Article 11 has to do with the transportation of arms and ammunition and the regime in force in that connection. I should like to draw your attention to Article 12. Let me read it. Paragraph 1: "A citizen of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina carrying weapons into or out of the HZ H-B shall report the weapons and ammunition to the border police or the military police at the state border". This is a highly complex provision, which implies several conclusions. First, that citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are treated here as aliens in relation to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; secondly, citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when entering or leaving the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, are actually crossing a state border, as is stated in this Article. So there are two major implications from this provision. To reiterate briefly, that citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are implicitly treated as foreigners and, secondly, that they are crossing a state border when entering or leaving the Croatian Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, you said that citizens who are not of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna are foreigners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that implicitly they are considered to be foreigners according to Article 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But what is the criterion of who is a foreigner and who is not? Is it just the fact that they are resident in Herceg-Bosna, or racial, a racial denominator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is not any racial reference as the citizenship is concerned. So I would answer to your question that just the residence would be a criteria for citizenship in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So if a Bosnian Muslim is resident in Herceg-Bosna, is he a citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would be treated as a citizen of HZ H-B in this case, but we are not, as of yet, in the area of citizenship, citizenship of HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "not yet"? You will come to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a document that deals with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment this can be translated as -- the term in my language is "Grain HZ H-B", less citoyens of HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I will wait for your document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may at this point, in the Serbian, Croatian or Bosnian language there is a small complication when talking about citizenship. Actually in the English language someone may be a British national, which in my language would mean a British citizen, but he may also be a Scotsman or a Welshman. In our languages, however, there is this term that we call "nation" and "nationality". Someone may be a Muslim by nationality, as you said, while at the same time being a citizen, having citizenship in this case of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Therefore in the languages I have mentioned, Croatian, Serbian and Bosnian, there is a clear distinction between ethnicity, which we call nationality, and citizenship. There are two terms for these two different conditions, but in English I always come across this problem in my papers and in my lectures that in the English language a national can mean either a citizen or a particular ethnic background of a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then my question is: who is a foreigner in this text number 13? Foreign citizens, who are the foreign citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Implicitly again foreign citizens according to Article 12 are people who have residence out of the HZ H-B, who are residing out of the territory of HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. Anybody who is residing out, whether he is a Serb, a Croat or an Englishman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, have you got any other questions? Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, I invite you to look at Articles 18 and 19 and more particularly at the first two lines of each provision. Would you say there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, up to this point I haven't made this clarification, but the French Judge does not have a translation of this text. It will help me in my English and my neighbour on the right could help me, but if we are going to talk about this a long time I would like to have a translation. It's not particularly urgent, but I would like both to be able to understand the scope of my colleagues' questions as well as the answer from the witness, because I have a stopped at Article 9 here. That is the translation stops at Article 9. That is what I would like to point out. This is not the question, of course, but perhaps in your answer you could give further clarifications as to what these Articles consist of and in the time being I will ask my colleagues to help me, and I can also ask the Prosecutor to promise me in the next few days to give me a translation of this, which is very important, because it does mark for the Prosecution that there was really a real interstate border system. Now again, Judge Shahabuddeen, would you mind repeating your question and also give some further details. I will try to get along as best I can with the help of Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I commiserate with the President for being as handicapped as he is. Certainly I should feel that very strongly if I were deprived of an English translation, which is the only language that unfortunately I know. I am at Articles 18 and 19, and I shall read the first two lines of Article 18: "Citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may move and sojourn in the border area only if they have an appropriate permit", which I take it as a permit to be issued by the authorities of the Croatian Community. So you have a reference there to citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a reference to movement and sojourning in the area. Now, in 19 you have a reading which runs this way: "A foreign citizen may move and sojourn in the border area only if he has obtained a permit from the competent authority or is crossing the border with a valid travel document". So you have two ideas here now -- several ideas but two relevant ones. You have a reference to a foreign citizen as distinguished from the reference in Article 18 to a citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you have a reference here now to crossing the border. This reference to crossing the border occurs in conjunction with a reference to a foreign citizen. Now, do you see any sort of distinction between a reference to citizens of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Article 18 and a reference to a foreign citizen in Article 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my view there is no difference between these two provisions that you have cited. The first provision that you cited in Article 18, which reads: "Citizens of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may move and sojourn in the border area only if they have an appropriate permit". However, after all, in my view the implication is that the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are treated as foreigners in relation to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, because if that were not so, then they would not need a special permit for movement and sojourn in the border area. Actually they have a virtually identical treatment as foreigners, which are mentioned in abstract terms, in Article 19, which may also move and sojourn in the border area only if they have obtained a permit from the competent body or if they are crossing the border with a valid travel document. Therefore, I see no distinction between these two concepts: citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and foreigners in relation to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Again, Professor Pajic, who are the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Isn't the Croatian Community part of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is a part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the extent to which it wishes to be that on the basis of these documents that I have been quoting throughout my testimony; in other words, by all these documents, by establishing separate bodies of authority, separate institutional, autonomous state structures, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is slowly, gradually but in a continuous manner indicating its intention to separate from The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the argument that I wish to set forth here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The argument is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, my apologies for the abridged translations in the French before you. Certainly I will ensure that you have a full translation of that document within the next few days, and if there are any of the others which are slightly abridged following on from there that you require full translations of, please indicate to me and I will have them done for me as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I can now refer you to document 11, which is a decree on implementing the law on the movement and residence of aliens in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war, could you give your comments on this document to the court? I know it is related to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a decree on the implementation on the law on the movement and residence of aliens in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna in times of war or the immediate threat of war. I shall very briefly draw your attention to a provision which will take us back to the debate we had a moment ago, your Honours. Actually the only inconsistency in the normative activities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that I have been able to discover is to be found in Article 2 of this decree. Article 2 says: "An alien, as provided for under this decree, shall be any person who is not a citizen of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina". Therefore, argumendum ad contrario, it can be established that citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina are not aliens in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. As I have said, this is an inconsistency in relation to the treatment enjoyed by citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the persons with residence in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is inconsistent with the treatment provided for in the previous decree on border crossings and sojourn regarding citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that decree. I do not wish to speculate on this matter at all, but I would say that there was a certain amount of hesitation on the part of the legislator at this point in time, in February 1993, when this decree was passed, to treat other citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as aliens in relation to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is there another interpretation possible? One assumes that the citizens of the Croatian Community are considered to be citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the contradiction that you have pointed out would be less apparent then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Croatian ethnicity with residence in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina outside the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna are treated as citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are large numbers of population of Croatian ethnic origin who are living particularly in urban centres of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in towns such as Sarajevo, I assume, Zenica, Tuzla and others, which are outside Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Are they also citizens of Herceg-Bosna? Is it some kind of dual nationality or dual citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is still premature to talk about dual citizenship or the possibility of a dual citizenship. It is true, however, that during the war, and we are talking of 1993, that persons of Croatian ethnic origin residing in The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could easily obtain a passport of the Republic of Croatia, because of their ethnic origin. Now I'm going beyond the framework of these documents, because they do not cover this question, but they are the fruit of my personal experience. For many citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was the only way under conditions of a terrible surroundings and conditions in which certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina were during the war, the only way of getting out of that environment was by obtaining a Croatian passport, because that passport permitted the holder to go to the Republic of Croatia, and also to many third countries without requiring a visa very often. I could elaborate further on this matter, if you wish, but that would be the crux of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor, may I put to you a sort of general question? If it is too general in nature, do not hesitate to tell me that. I understand your evidence to be directed to establishing that the process was in the course of creating a separate state with accompanying state apparatus, but at any particular stage the exact position reached by that process might differ from the position which it might reach at another stage of the process. Is my appreciation of your evidence correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your appreciation is very correct. This evolution of the legal system, of the legal order of Herceg-Bosna is something that I view from the very outset as a continued process, which, of course, does have it ups and downs, if I may say so, and, of course, it depends on the development of the political situation in Herceg-Bosna itself and the situation in the entire environment, and also the situation concerning war operations in 1992 and 1993. It is quite certain that this was not always a smooth process, so your appreciation is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, would you go on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One last question on this document, Dr. Pajic, and I will be calling on the fruits of your more extensive knowledge beyond these documents but it is a simple point. This document, in effect, regulates the movement of aliens, which are defined by Article 2 under this decree. It regulates their movement within this entity. What was the position at law in the former Yugoslavia about the free movement of the people between the different constituent states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What document are we talking about? Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are talking about page 2 of the decree on the law on movement and residence of aliens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aliens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, document 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, because there are two similar documents, one dealing with the movement of aliens and the other of the movement of nationals or citizens within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That's why I was confused. The decree on implementing the law on the movement and residence of aliens in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna stipulates quite strictly that an alien, for example, in Article 6 who wishes to reside temporarily in the HZ H-B should submit a request for such temporary residence permit immediately upon entering the HZ H-B. I think in this case we can talk about a legacy, so to speak, from the former Yugoslavia. On the one hand, the movement of foreigners in the territory of the former Yugoslavia was not subject to such strict control as was the case in other countries of east and central Europe, especially the Soviet Union. On the other hand, there was a system according to which aliens were supposed to register in the places where they would stay, in the hotel where they would stay or in tourist organisations, if they were spending their vacations there, etc. So this is a practice that was valid beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But strictly was there control within the former Yugoslavia between the constituent republics, or was passage between the republics free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not, but as far as citizens of that country were concerned, the former Yugoslavia, there was unlimited freedom of movement practically from one region to the other, from one republic to another, from one city to another, again as opposed to the situation in the former Soviet Union, where people had to be granted various approvals. They had to register when they left, when they came, etc., etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. If we could move on, now to document 12, which introduces the concepts of residency and domicile, if you could make some brief comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In connection with the previous decree I mentioned the situation in which the citizens of the former Yugoslavia had full freedom of movement within their own country. They could change their place of residence. They could travel either on business or private matters. They could leave their place of residence without any special restrictions. I think that that is the situation here in this decree, too, although very strictly Article 5 says that: "Citizens having the status of a refugee or displaced person in the territory of HZ H-B and other citizens whose domicile was in their place of residence until 1st April 1992 shall retain their place of domicile". This is nevertheless a strict control over where refugees are or persons who were displaced. So we are talking about refugees and displaced persons. It is stipulated that the place of residence they have -- de jure practically as their place of residence they have that which they had before 1st April 1992, probably in the hope they would go back to the place where they lived before that date or from which they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 13, I think you can deal with this document very briefly. It is a further decision on preferential treatment of goods imported from The Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say the same thing that I said concerning the previous decision that dealt with this subject matter. Again this means an extension of preferential treatment of goods imported from The Republic of Croatia or goods originating from The Republic of Croatia. It says that a special decree on customs tariffs will not be applied in the case of such goods. May I highlight once again that this is something that is done by a state towards another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to -- if I could give you -- I'm sorry. If we could continue with that document and if you could give the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on the import of goods from the Republic of Croatia is dated 9th April 1993, and it was signed by the President of the HVO of the HZ H-B. Perhaps I should have done this before, but with your permission I wish to say that practically all documents, all decisions that were published in the Official Gazette contain a final provision saying that: "This decree shall enter into force on the day it is issued". In Yugoslav legal tradition this is quite unusual, because again, thanks to continental European legal legacy, in the former Yugoslav legislation, legislation would usually enter into force seven days upon publication in the Official Gazette, and on that basis I draw the conclusion that these were rather urgent measures invariably, that norms were needed and certain social relations had to be regulated as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could refer you to Article 14, which is the decision on carrying out mobilisation, if you could make some brief comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on carrying out mobilisation in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in times of immediate threat of war or in wartime was adopted on 10th June 1993 and it was signed by the President of the HVO of the HZ H-B, Mr. Jadranko Perlic. Again, this is my opinion that this is a document adopted by a state. I do not know of a single case from International Law of War that mobilisation was ever declared by a non-state entry, so by its very definition an act of mobilisation is passed by a sovereign state. Actually this decision carries out in practice the previous document on the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is the decree on the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, which was adopted in July 1992. This is practically all I would have to say in this connection. Of course, as in any document on mobilisation, a certain procedure is mentioned here, how men of military age are supposed to report, various departments, etc. In this connection I just wish to remind you that The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a year before that, on 20th June 1992, declared mobilisation as it was faced by aggression, as was then designed by the Yugoslav people's army. This mobilisation was declared on 20th June 1992 and the act on mobilisation was published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina number 7 from 1992 on page 234. Due to my professional interests I started following these new developments in the legislation of the states that were created on the territory of the former Yugoslavia at a very early stage, and that is how I received these official gazettes too. Yesterday in my introductory remarks, when I spoke of my professional experience, I mentioned that, too, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now refer you to document 15. Specifically this decree concerns the rights and obligations of citizens of Herceg-Bosna working abroad, and their particular commitment to the defence obligation, and I wondered if specifically you could explain this rather odd provision in this decree concerning the financial obligation of those living abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna by this decree actually prescribed the obligation of all its citizens temporarily working abroad, that they should contribute through certain material resources to the defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say that all of those who are temporarily abroad, as they say here, and whose permanent residence is on the territory of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say on the territory of the HZ H-B, are duty bound by this decree to contribute a certain monetary amount which is stipulated here. They shall pay 300 Deutschmarks to the HVO in the municipality of their permanent current place of residence anywhere in the world. It is interesting to note the consistent thought that was given to financing the needs of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Defence needs in particular, and the extent to which this budget policy, if I may call it that, was taken into account. This decision was adopted on 9th April 1993. However, this obligation mentioned in Article 3 was backdated to 1st April 1992. So paragraph 2 of Article 3 reads as follows and I quote: "The obligation to pay the above amount shall be applied as of 1st April 1992". So that is to say a year back. These obligations had to be met. A later decision that was published in the Official Gazette number 14 of 1993, we find a decision that as far as these dues are concerned for the period from April 1992 until April 1993, a lump sum was supposed to be paid by all citizens to the amount of 4,800 Deutschmarks as their overdue obligations vis-à-vis the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, under this document of 9th April 1993, am I correct in saying that failure to meet this financial obligation was regarded as equivalent to avoidance of military service within Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Article 6 contains the following provision and I quote: "Avoiding payment of the financial obligation described in Article 2 of this decree shall be considered equivalent to avoiding service in the armed forces and shall incur sanctions as stipulated in the corresponding regulations on avoiding service in the armed forces".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, although it doesn't strictly run in the order of the documents, could I refer you next to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. Dr. Shahabuddeen would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This is interesting. Am I right in my impression of your earlier evidence that Croatians resident in Bosnia-Herzegovina outside of the HZ H-B would be regarded in the HZ H-B citizens of the HZ H-B? If that is correct, would those Croatians resident in Bosnia-Herzegovina outside of the HZ H-B be regarded as citizens of the Croatian Community to whom this decree would apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, would you go on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could refer you, Dr. Pajic, to document 17 first. Although it actually comes in terms of date order after document 16, I think it's a more correct manner of dealing with things. This is the basic decision on establishing and proclaiming the Croatian Republic, republic as opposed to community, of Herceg-Bosna. Could you explain this document to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is document 17, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please note that there are many documents here. I do not have 13, 14, 15, 16. This is 17 now. Please note that as well and then go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you would continue, Dr. Pajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the process of the construction of statehood of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna we reach a stage when on 28th August 1993 this decision was adopted called "Basic Decision on Establishing and Proclaiming the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna". This means a departure from the previous name, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was probably no longer suited to this developed state and legal structure that developed in the territory of this entity, and a decision was passed on the proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I think this marks a formal and legal completion of a process that I have tried to illustrate in the course of my testimony, because finally Herceg-Bosna is established as a state community. I say this because such a decision has to be viewed in the context of the events linked to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. I should like to underline that after the collapse of the Yugoslav Federation all states emerging from the former Yugoslavia retained attached to their name the attribute "republic", The Republic of Slovenia, The Republic of Croatia, The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and finally The Republic of Macedonia. We will not go into difficulties linked to the name of an international legal nature, considering the position it has. It is very important to note that each of the entities that aspired to proclaiming itself a republic within the former Yugoslavia retained this attribute of republic, because thereby it was on an equal level with all the other states emerging from the former Yugoslavia. So that is one point I wish to make. Another has to do with the preamble of this decision, which is very meaningful. It is a strongly expressed nationalist rhetoric, noting that this is a republic of the Croatian people, and what I find is lacking in a preamble of this kind, since emphasis is placed on the national character of this republic, at least a line is lacking regarding the rights and freedoms of minorities, and there are no such provisions in the documents that I have analysed. Let me mention just two provisions of this decision, and that is Article 2, which says that: "The territory of the Republic shall encompass the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna". That is what was initially established as the territory. That is the group of municipalities. I think there were 30 of them. " The final borders" -- I am quoting -- "shall be determined by the constitution of the Republic".
