This, in my opinion, leaves the door open regarding the question of the borders of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which could be interpreted as an aspiration towards including certain other territories that were not originally included according to the original act on the foundation of the Croatian Community, and Article 10, which refers to Mostar, which was formerly of the centre of the community, now it is described as "the capital of the republic ".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if I can now refer you very briefly back to document 17, which is the decision on the constitution on the House of Representatives, if you could briefly explain that document to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has to do with the constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I interrupt you? It's document 16. My apologies. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a decision on constituting the house of representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Therefore actually it has to do with the establishment of the highest representative body in The Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It is what one might call a Parliament of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I shall quote Article 1: "The House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna shall be the supreme representative body vested with legislative power in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna". I beg your pardon. Forgive me for this pause. Article 2 is noteworthy because it says: "Pending the first free and democratic elections, the representatives of the House of Representatives shall be representatives of the Croatian people in the Chamber of Municipalities of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna". We see here the introduction of the ethnic element regarding the right to represent the people in the House of Representatives; in other words, the passive right to vote, the right to be elected to a House of Representatives belongs, according to this decision, only in the Croatian people, people of Croatian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Briefly, Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to Article 19, which concerns the transfer of the powers of the Presidency of the Croatian Community --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: -- into the House of Representatives, what are your comments on that provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 19 is actually the logical consequence of the constitution of the House of Representatives, because let me remind you that the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had legislative powers, and now these powers, according to this decision, are taken over by the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic, so that the competencies of the Presidency cease here and are being taken over by the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Since the Presidency originally consisted -- a constituent element of the Presidency was the HVO, was the HVO effectively being transferred into the House of Representatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 2 says that until the first democratic elections, the representatives of the House of Representatives will consist, among others, of members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which includes HVO members. Therefore, it can be said that the House of Representatives includes members of the HVO, because the Presidency continues to be a constituent part of the House of Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now move on, please, Dr. Pajic, to document 18, which is a declaration on the adoption of documents on the protection and exercise of human freedoms and rights? If you could give the date of this document and the signatory. I do not want you to read every single provision of this decision, but can you highlight for the court the important areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. The declaration on the adoption of documents on the protection and exercise of human rights and freedoms was adopted by the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on 30th July 1993. Let me say straightaway that this is a customary declaration for all states that emerged in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. All the constitutions contain such reference to basic human rights or rather the legal instruments governing human rights. This declaration lists 19 of them. If you examine closely the list of all these international documents, you will see that they cover what is considered today to be the core of international law governing human rights, starting from the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, through what is known as the Bill of Rights, that is the universal declaration on human rights, the Geneva Conventions on Human Rights, to specific documents linked to human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 19, Dr. Pajic, which I think is a decision on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. I thought that the witness was speaking about B, the protection of ethnic groups and minorities. Very, very briefly, because you said before that in the preamble of the constitution nothing was said about ethnic groups or minorities and perhaps this is the place you would explain the difference that took place as time went by or is this simply what is ordinarily put in this type of declaration, this type of protection that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention to chapter B of this declaration, which refers to two documents devoted to rights of minorities, but neither of these documents, neither the recommendation of the European Council and the Parliamentary Assembly on the rights of minorities, nor the United Nations' declaration on the rights of members of national, ethnic, religious and linguistic minorities are internationally binding documents. One is a recommendation and the other is a declaration. They stipulate certain standards in international law for treatment of minorities but they are not binding on states because they do not have the character of a contract. Therefore, I can still allege that in the constitution and legal documents of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna there are no specific operational provisions on the protection of minorities living in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. There is no reference to the rights and freedoms that minorities and members of non-Croatian peoples would enjoy in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Allow me also to say that this declaration, in my view, is a very positive one in the process of development of the legal system of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, because it is new in relation to previous legal documents, as it is devoid of nationalistic rhetoric and reference to historical claims. So I think that this declaration is the fruit of a good legal or legal/political instinct of the legislators of the Croatian Republic. It was the right time, that is the summer of 1993, to pass a decision of this time. Since I remember this period well in the peace process initiated by the international community, this declaration was also the upshot of pressure on the part of the international negotiators who were trying to stop the war in Bosnia Herzegovina. Let us not forget that at that time representatives of the Croatian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were participating in the peace negotiations within the framework of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia in Geneva co-chaired by Messrs Vance and Owen and later Messrs Stoltenberg and Owen. So I assume that this declaration was also part of the political environment surrounding the representatives of the Croatian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think just to conclude on this document, it shows an awareness of global obligations under international humanitarian law by the drafters of these documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, though the implementation of these general documents of international law is lacking, that is their transformation into national legislation, but it is an indication of the acceptance of the general instruments on human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now proceed to document 19, which is the decision on the appointment of the commission for investigation of war crimes. Can you give your general comments on this document to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also describe this decision as a progressive one in the process of evolution of the legal system in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So now it is called HR H-B. That is the formation of a commission for the investigation of war crimes. Of course, war crimes that occurred in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So I think that this, too, reflects a feeling of obligation, legal and political obligation, towards the peace process under the sponsorship of the international community. The decision was passed in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 20, which is the decision on the establishment of a presidential council. If you could make some brief comments about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision on establishing the presidential council of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was passed on December 10th, 1993 and it is followed by a series of decisions on appointments made and signed by the President of the Croatian Republic, Mr. Mate Boban, who at the same time nominates members of the presidential council, that is members of his council. Since the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna has been constituted, the President of Herceg-Bosna remains as an individual, as a head of state, in this case, the implementing the practice of the latter day history of the former Yugoslavia, that is from the 1970s onwards, a collective council is formed to advise the President in the process of performing his functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could now refer you to document 21, and we get back to the subject of citizenship again, a short decision. If you could give the Tribunal your comments on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decree taking over the decree with the force of law on the citizenship of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me point out that in our legal practice decree actually provided the legal procedure for acquiring citizenship. What was the procedure for naturalisation, the time period required, the special conditions and so on, that was the contents of the decree on citizenship of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So taking over those provisions means taking over the procedural mechanism for the acquisition of citizenship of the Republic -- of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It has no other function, as can be seen from the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A question from Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As far as military service was concerned, was it imposed on everyone within the borders of the community of -- of the Croatian community, or was there a criterion based on ethnicity or anything in the choice of people to do the military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Sorry. I shouldn't speak in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The criterion for military service was based actually on permanent residence in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The ethnic element is not mentioned in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In that respect, Judge Riad, if I could refer you to document 14, Article 1, which is the foundation for what Dr. Pajic is saying, it talks about the concept of permanent residence within the Croatian Community. Lastly, Dr. Pajic, if I could refer you to document 22, which is part of the Official Gazette of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I wonder if you could, first of all, distinguish for the court the origin of this document as compared to the origin of the documents which we have referred to up to this point before actually explaining the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far in my testimony I have been speaking exclusively about documents and on the basis of the documents published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I now have before me a document published on 18th September 1992 in a different edition, in a different publication, which is the official publication carrying laws, enactments and decisions of state organs. I'm referring to the Official Gazette of The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, number 16, in which a decision was published of the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which responded -- I beg your pardon. The decision was taken on 14th September, the decision of the constitutional court, which was reacting to a decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and to several other decisions which laid the foundations for the legal order and bodies of authority within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina assessed that all the decisions listed in the preamble of this decision which you have before you --- the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community; the decision on changes and amendments to that decision; the statutory decision on temporary establishment of executive authority; the decree on the organisation, operation and jurisdiction of the judicial authorities in the event of war on the armed forces of the Croatian Community; the decree on the reimbursement of salaries and other financial reimbursements to members of the armed forces; the decree on the take-over of the resources of the former JNA; the decree on the appropriation and transfer of ownership to the Croatian Community of property owned by the occupying force; the decree on public enterprises in the Croatian Community -- all these decisions were annulled by decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather they were declared unconstitutional in relation to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Constitutional Court found these decisions to be in violation of the valid constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the ruling of the Constitutional Court, the articles of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina are referred to, that is the 1979 Constitution with the amendments of 1991, which were passed after the first democratic and multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, held in November 1990. I could say in reference to this decision of the Constitutional Court that it cites the appropriate provisions of the constitution, declaring the decisions of the Croatian Community unconstitutional, and it is also important to note the dry legal language. It is extremely legalistic, without any excessive rhetoric. It refers to constitutional provisions and the chapters of the constitution that were violated by the decisions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Let me end by saying that in these documents taken from the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna I did not come across any kind of official reaction on the part of anybody of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to this decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina which annulled all those decisions up to September 1992 declaring them unconstitutional in terms of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, it's now 1 o'clock. We can stop here. The interpreters have worked very hard. I would like to know how you see things going forward tomorrow morning between 1 o'clock and 1 o'clock. Do you have any other questions you want to ask? How do you wish to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We thought, your Honour, that we would finish with Dr. Pajic's general conclusions, an overview of all of the documents, which we establish will be about fifteen minutes, and then after that we would, of course, offer the witness for cross-examination by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then that is how we will proceed. We can now suspend our hearing and begin with the same witness tomorrow for his conclusion and the cross-examination. We are suspending the hearing now and we will resume tomorrow at 10 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: --ooOoo--

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock)
